Do the SPLIT itself with Fable — splitting the PLAN into epics is the judgement that shapes everything after it. Before that split is final, ask the question consultant (ask_consultants) what matters in this plan and where — if none answers, say so and decide — name the cornerstone areas, and write the epics at the bottom of the plan. A plan split straight into stories, with no epics, is split by Fable too: its stories go at the bottom of the plan, and at most one of them is a cornerstone. Then split each EPIC into stories on Opus, one stories document per epic, marking its CORNERSTONE stories — where being wrong is expensive: payments, money, architecture, data migration, a public contract — at most 2·E/5 rounded up for a plan of E epics (1–2 epics: 1, 3–5: 2, 6–7: 3). Every story that is not a cornerstone: Opus writes the test scenarios and the brief (what to change and how), Sonnet writes the code, the fixes and the unit and integration tests, and Opus reviews it — every reviewer, judge, architect and finding verifier runs on Opus. A cornerstone story, and any security work — cryptography, authentication, authorisation, outside that quota — gets its spec (the scenarios and the brief) from Fable, its review from Opus and its code from Sonnet. You write code yourself only for a change to ONE file of at most 50 changed lines; anything bigger goes to a subagent on Sonnet. Search and research go to scouts on Sonnet: 1.5·N rounded up where N would have run on Opus (1→2, 2→3, 3→5), each with its own focus. Always the newest version of each model: pass it by its alias, never a versioned id. If Fable is refused on a spend or session limit, continue on Opus and say so. In your summary, name the model each role and each story ran on, and how many agents ran on each model.
